section.title: The Suffering Servant
section.sectionRationale: This is the summit of the Book of Comfort and arguably of the entire Old Testament's witness to Christ, the fourth and final Servant Song. Everything Isaiah has been building toward, the arm of the LORD bared, the good news proclaimed, the exile answered, gathers here into a single figure who is despised, pierced, crushed, silent before His accusers, and yet exalted above all. No Old Testament passage is quoted or echoed by the New Testament writers about Jesus more directly or more often.
section.thesis: The Servant of the LORD bears, in His own body and by God's own will, the guilt, punishment, and sickness that belonged to His people, dying an unjust death as a guilt offering for the many, and is afterward raised to see His offspring, prolong His days, and divide the spoils, because His substitutionary suffering has already succeeded.
section.frameNote: Five movements: the Servant exalted though disfigured; who has believed this report; a man of sorrows despised and stricken; He was pierced for our transgressions; and the aftermath, a grave with the rich, offspring, and intercession for the transgressors.

units.label: The Servant exalted though disfigured
units.note: kings will shut their mouths because of Him

verses.text: Behold, My {{ebed|Servant}} will prosper; He will be raised and lifted up and highly exalted.
Just as many were appalled at Him, His appearance was disfigured beyond that of any man, and His form was marred beyond human likeness,
so He will {{nazah|sprinkle}} many nations. Kings will shut their mouths because of Him. For they will see what they have not been told, and they will understand what they have not heard.

units.label: Who has believed our message
units.note: no beauty that we should desire Him

verses.text: Who has believed our message? And to whom has the arm of the LORD been revealed?
He grew up before Him like a tender shoot, and like a root out of dry ground. He had no stately form or majesty to attract us, no beauty that we should desire Him.
He was despised and rejected by men, a man of sorrows, acquainted with grief. Like one from whom men hide their faces, He was despised, and we esteemed Him not.

units.label: Pierced for our transgressions
units.note: the punishment that brought us peace

verses.text: Surely He took on our infirmities and carried our sorrows; yet we considered Him stricken by God, struck down and afflicted.
But He was pierced for our transgressions, He was crushed for our iniquities; the punishment that brought us peace was upon Him, and by His stripes we are healed.
We all like sheep have gone astray, each one has turned to his own way; and the LORD has laid upon Him the {{avon|iniquity}} of us all.
He was oppressed and afflicted, yet He did not open His mouth. He was led like a lamb to the slaughter, and as a sheep before her shearers is silent, so He did not open His mouth.
By oppression and judgment He was taken away, and who can recount His descendants? For He was cut off from the land of the living; He was stricken for the transgression of My people.

units.label: A guilt offering for the many

verses.text: He was assigned a grave with the wicked, and with a rich man in His death, although He had done no violence, nor was any deceit in His mouth.

Yet it was the LORD’s will to crush Him and to cause Him to suffer; and when His soul is made a {{asham|guilt offering}}, He will see His offspring, He will prolong His days, and the good pleasure of the LORD will prosper in His hand.
After the anguish of His soul, He will see the light of life and be satisfied. By His knowledge My righteous Servant will justify {{rabbim|many}}, and He will bear their iniquities.

units.label: Numbered with the transgressors
units.note: He poured out His life unto death

verses.text: Therefore I will allot Him a portion with the great, and He will divide the spoils with the strong, because He has poured out His life unto death, and He was numbered with the transgressors. Yet He bore the sin of many and made intercession for the transgressors.

ebed.gloss: Servant, one who belongs to and serves another. Across Isaiah 40 to 53 this title deepens from Israel's calling to a single figure who succeeds where Israel fails, culminating here in a Servant who is exalted precisely through humiliation and death, then raised and highly exalted, Philippians 2:8-9.

nazah.gloss: To sprinkle, the verb used for priestly sprinkling of blood in atonement rituals, Leviticus 4 and 16. The Servant will sprinkle many nations, language that casts His coming exaltation in priestly, cleansing terms, He purifies the nations by what He suffers.

avon.gloss: Iniquity, guilt, the twisted moral weight of sin and its consequence together. The LORD causes the avon of us all to strike, literally to meet or converge upon, the Servant, a picture of guilt being transferred rather than merely observed or forgiven in the abstract.

asham.gloss: Guilt offering, the specific Levitical sacrifice for offenses requiring restitution, Leviticus 5-7. The Servant's soul is made an asham, the only place in the Old Testament where a person, rather than an animal, becomes this sacrifice, marking His death as substitutionary atonement in the most technical sacrificial vocabulary Israel had.

rabbim.gloss: The many, a term used three times in this chapter, verses 11 and 12, for those whose iniquities the Servant bears and whom He justifies. It signals a vast, though not necessarily universal, scope of substitution, echoed by Jesus Himself, His life a ransom for many, Mark 10:45, and Paul's for many will be made righteous, Romans 5:19.

basic.context: This is the fourth and final Servant Song, and it stands at the theological center of the entire Old Testament. A figure appears who is despised, disfigured, silent before His accusers, and put to death, yet whose suffering is described as bearing the sins of others and satisfying God's own will, after which He is raised and exalted.
basic.hermeneutics: Jewish and Christian readers have long debated who this Servant is, Israel corporately, a righteous prophet, or the coming Messiah. The New Testament writers read it directly and repeatedly of Jesus, and this study takes that reading seriously and honestly, while naming the older debate rather than hiding it.
basic.originalLanguages: The Servant, ebed, will sprinkle, nazah, many nations, priestly language for cleansing. He carries our avon, iniquity, and His soul becomes an asham, a guilt offering, the technical Levitical sacrifice for sin requiring restitution, here offered by a person rather than an animal. He justifies the rabbim, the many, bearing their sin.
basic.typology: Every detail points forward: the lamb led silently to slaughter, the grave with the rich, the guilt offering made of a life, the intercession for transgressors. The New Testament does not merely allude to this chapter, it treats it as prophecy fulfilled in specific, verifiable detail in the arrest, trial, death, burial, and vindication of Jesus.
basic.christ: Philip explains this very passage to the Ethiopian eunuch and tells him the good news about Jesus, Acts 8:32-35. Peter says Christ suffered for us, bearing our sins in His body, by whose stripes we are healed, quoting verse 5 outright, 1 Peter 2:22-25. Matthew ties Jesus' healing ministry to verse 4, Matthew 8:17. Jesus applies verse 12 to Himself directly the night before He dies, Luke 22:37, He was numbered with the transgressors.
basic.god: God is both the Judge whose justice required that sin be punished, and the Giver who provided, at infinite cost to Himself, the very Servant who bears that punishment. It was the LORD's will to crush Him, a hard truth that this study does not soften, because only in owning it do we see how much God loved us in the doing.
basic.crossReferences: Acts 8:32-35 has Philip preach Jesus straight from this chapter. 1 Peter 2:22-25 quotes it of Christ's sinless, substitutionary suffering. Matthew 8:17 applies verse 4 to Jesus' healing ministry. Luke 22:37 has Jesus quote verse 12 of Himself before His arrest.
basic.oneStory: Every sacrifice, every psalm of the righteous sufferer, every promise that God would deal with sin, converges here: a Servant crushed for the guilt of others, silent before His accusers, buried with the rich, then raised to see His offspring and divide the spoils. This is the center of the Bible's one story, told centuries before it happened, and fulfilled in Jesus Christ.

context.literary:
The fourth Song is a carefully built poem of five stanzas of three verses each, 52:13 to 15, 53:1 to 3, 53:4 to 6, 53:7 to 9 and 53:10 to 12. The first and the last stanza frame the rest with the same story told in the same order: the Servant is exalted. In the opening stanza the LORD speaks and announces success before it describes anything else, 'My Servant will prosper'. In the closing stanza the LORD speaks again and promises a portion with the great. Between them the voice changes to 'we', a group of speakers who confess that they misjudged Him. That 'we' is the heart of the poem. The reader overhears the confession of those who looked at the Servant, saw a stricken man and concluded that God had struck Him for His own sins.

The poem moves in a deliberate arc. It begins with the high position, 'raised and lifted up and highly exalted', then drops into the deepest humiliation, disfigurement, rejection, a cut-off life and a grave, and then rises again at the end. The three verbs at the start, raised, lifted up and exalted, are the same terms Isaiah used in 6:1 when he saw the LORD 'high and exalted'. John makes the connection explicit when he says that Isaiah saw Jesus' glory and spoke about Him, John 12:41. The Servant is being described in language that was used for the LORD Himself.

Within the middle stanzas there is a movement from the outer to the inner. The second stanza describes how He looked, with no stately form and no beauty. The third describes what He carried, infirmities, sorrows, transgressions, iniquities. The fourth tells of what was done to Him, oppression, silence, a grave. The sharp turn is at the centre. 53:4 has 'Surely He took on our infirmities', and in 53:5 and 6 the repeated 'our' and 'us' is set against the single 'Him'. Every phrase of verse 5 is balanced: pierced for our transgressions, crushed for our iniquities, punishment for our peace, stripes for our healing.

Verse 6 gathers the whole confession into one picture of sheep who have gone astray, 'each one has turned to his own way', answered by a single line in which the LORD lays on Him the iniquity of us all. The poem is a drama of two ways: the many going their own way, and the One going the way that is laid on Him.

Many scholars also note a gap between 53:9 and 53:10, where the poem's tone changes from lament to purpose. Up to verse 9 the Servant has been acted on. From verse 10 the LORD speaks of His 'will' and the Servant begins to see, prolong and be satisfied. The suffering is not the end of the story, and the poem's last line returns to the very thing the poem began with, the Servant's exaltation.
context.historical:
The poem comes from the same exilic setting as the rest of Isaiah 40 to 55. The exiles had lived with the sense that their suffering was the result of their sin, and the words of 53:4, that the onlookers considered Him 'stricken by God', reflected a view that was common in Israel, in which suffering signalled divine disfavour. Job's friends held that view, and the book of Job exists partly to challenge it. The Servant is a righteous man who suffers, and the poem refuses to treat His pain as proof of His guilt.

The Old Testament had several categories that the first hearers would have used to understand His death. The most direct is the guilt offering, the asham of 53:10, described in Leviticus 5:14 to 16 as a ram brought to deal with an offence against holy things and accompanied by restitution of the value plus a fifth. The detail of restitution matters. An asham paid back what was owed. A second picture is the Day of Atonement, in which the high priest laid his hands on a live goat and confessed over it all the iniquities of the people, and the goat 'carried on itself all their iniquities' into the wilderness, Leviticus 16:21 and 22. The same Hebrew verb to carry or bear is used of the Servant in 53:4 and 53:12.

A third background is the lamb, whose silence in 53:7 would have recalled sacrifice, the shearing, and Jeremiah's own description of himself as 'a gentle lamb led to slaughter', Jeremiah 11:19. The figure of the shepherd and sheep in 53:6 belongs to the same field of imagery as the prophets' picture of Israel's leaders as failed shepherds, Ezekiel 34, and of God as the true shepherd who comes to seek the lost, Ezekiel 34:11 and 12.

The burial detail in 53:9 needs a note of caution. The standard Hebrew text gives a grave 'with the wicked' and 'with a rich man in His death'. The way a criminal's body was handled in Israel was shaped by Deuteronomy 21:22 and 23, which required that a hanged man be buried the same day. In the first century this was literally carried out when a wealthy disciple, Joseph of Arimathea, asked for the body of Jesus and laid it in his own new tomb, Matthew 27:57 to 60.

Since the Servant is called 'My Servant' and the surrounding Songs have already spoken of kings who will see and bow, Isaiah 49:7, the original audience would have understood that the answer to the shame of the exile would involve a figure whose shame is reversed before the nations.
context.canonical:
No chapter of the Old Testament is more heavily used by the New. Within the poem's own movement it grows out of the previous Songs: the Servant who is a covenant and a light to the nations in 42:6, who is despised and abhorred but honoured by kings in 49:7, and who gives His back to those who strike Him in 50:6. Its opening verse, with its question about the arm of the LORD, is the answer to the 'arm' of 51:9 and 52:10.

The New Testament quotes it or leans on it again and again. John applies 53:1 to the unbelief that met Jesus' signs, John 12:37 to 41, and Paul applies it to Israel's response to the gospel, Romans 10:16. Paul uses 52:15 as the basis of his mission to those who had not heard, Romans 15:20 and 21. Matthew reads 53:4 in the healing ministry, Matthew 8:16 and 17. Peter unpacks verses 5 and 6 in his teaching on the cross, 1 Peter 2:22 to 25, which also draws on 53:9 for the sinlessness of Christ. Luke records Jesus applying 53:12 to Himself on the eve of the cross, Luke 22:37, and Acts 8:32 to 35 shows Philip beginning at Isaiah 53 and telling the Ethiopian eunuch the good news of Jesus.

Further allusions are widely recognised even where the verses are not cited word for word. Paul's summary 'Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures', 1 Corinthians 15:3, and 'He was delivered over to death for our trespasses and was raised to life for our justification', Romans 4:25, echo the twofold shape of the poem, death for sins and vindication after. Hebrews 9:28 speaks of Christ offered once 'to bear the sins of many', which borrows the language of 53:12. Jesus' own words that He came 'to give His life as a ransom for many', Mark 10:45 and Matthew 20:28, use the same idea of the one for the many that runs through the poem.

The poem also draws on older Scripture. The Servant's sprinkling in 52:15 recalls the sprinkling of blood in the sacrificial system, the guilt offering of 53:10 comes straight from Leviticus, and the lamb and sheep draw on the shepherd imagery of the prophets. These connections show that Isaiah is not inventing a new idea of atonement. He is bringing together the sacrificial system, the suffering of the righteous and the promise of a coming King and showing that one person will carry all three.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Isaiah's aim in this poem was to overturn his readers' assumptions about how God saves and who His chosen one is. Israel expected deliverance to look like power: the arm of the LORD in the sea, a warrior king, an army returning home. The prophet is asked to say that the arm of the LORD will be revealed in a man who looks weak, whose form was marred and whose death looked like divine punishment. That is why the poem begins with the response, 'Who has believed our message?' The prophet expected it to be hard to believe, and he says so before the evidence is given.

He also wanted his hearers to see the meaning of a suffering that could not be understood from the outside. The confession of 53:4 to 6 puts the reader in the place of those who misread the Servant's wounds. They thought He was being punished for His own faults; they now see that the wounds were for theirs. The author intends the reader to join that 'we'. He asks them to move from spectator to confessor, saying 'all we like sheep have gone astray'.

Finally he wanted to give them certainty about the outcome. Without the last stanza the poem would be a tragedy. With it, readers learn that the LORD takes pleasure in the Servant's work, that He will see His offspring and prolong His days, and that the many will be justified. The exiles needed to know that God would not waste a righteous man's suffering, and that His purposes for the world would prosper through that very suffering.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The poem is a description of what the Servant does and what God does through Him. It is not a command to others to suffer in the same way, and it does not make every instance of suffering atoning. The sufferings of believers cannot bear the sins of others. Peter makes the point carefully in 1 Peter 2:21 to 24, where Christ's death is a pattern to follow in how we respond to injustice, and also something He alone did: 'He Himself bore our sins in His body on the tree.' We are told to follow His example, 'He did not retaliate', but we are not told to bear the sin of anyone.

The poem also invites a response that is prescriptive in an indirect way. The people who speak in the first person plural are those who have realised their error. They are an example for the reader: acknowledge that we are the ones who went astray, that the stripes were meant for us, and that the LORD has laid our iniquity on another. The text ends in 53:11 with the promise that the Servant will justify many, and the wider New Testament shows that this justification is received by faith, Romans 3:25 and 26.

There is a further caution about verse 4. Matthew applies 'He took on our infirmities and carried our diseases' to the healings of Jesus, Matthew 8:17, and Peter applies 'by His stripes you are healed' to the healing of sin, 1 Peter 2:24. The passage does not promise that every illness will be cured in this life. It points to the cross as the ground of all healing, with its fullest result in the resurrection.

debates.question: Who is the Servant of Isaiah 53?

views.label: Jesus the Messiah
views.case: The New Testament applies the poem to Jesus, and Jesus applied 53:12 to Himself, Luke 22:37. Philip answers the eunuch's question, 'who is the prophet talking about, himself or someone else?', by starting at this passage and telling him about Jesus, Acts 8:34 and 35. The detail of the poem, a sinless sufferer who dies for the sins of the many and is vindicated, fits no one else. Christian interpreters have read it this way from the beginning.

views.label: Israel, the nation or the faithful remnant
views.case: Isaiah has called Israel the Servant in 49:3, and many Jewish commentators, especially in the medieval period, read the poem as Israel's suffering among the nations, with the nations as the speakers who finally recognise that Israel's affliction had a purpose. On this reading the 'we' are the nations and the poem is a vindication of a long-suffering people.

views.label: A prophet, or Isaiah himself
views.case: Others have proposed a righteous individual of the prophet's own day, even Isaiah or Jeremiah, whose suffering was understood in hindsight. They point to Jeremiah's lamb-like experience in Jeremiah 11:19.

debates.bearing: The wording of the poem works against the national view. The Servant is distinguished from 'my people' in 53:8, where He is stricken 'for the transgression of My people', and He dies and is not merely afflicted. The first-person 'we' confesses its own sin, so the speakers cannot be a righteous nation standing in the Servant's place. The Servant who suffers for Israel cannot be Israel. A prophet's life does not match the claim that He will justify many. The best fit is the one the New Testament names.

debates.question: What does the Servant's suffering accomplish?

views.label: A penal substitute: He bears the punishment for sin in the place of the many
views.case: The poem uses the language of transfer. He bears our iniquities, 53:11 and 12; He was pierced and crushed for them, 53:5; 'the LORD has laid upon Him the iniquity of us all', 53:6; and the punishment that brought us peace was upon Him. His soul is a guilt offering, 53:10, a sacrifice that deals with offence. The apostolic summary 'He bore our sins in His body on the tree', 1 Peter 2:24, 'Christ died for our sins', 1 Corinthians 15:3, and 'God made Him who knew no sin to be sin on our behalf', 2 Corinthians 5:21, read it as substitution.

views.label: A representative or solidarity: He identifies with the sinful and suffers their lot
views.case: Some stress that the Servant stands with the many rather than in place of them, numbered with the transgressors and sharing in their suffering. He enters the world of the guilty and brings them through it, so that His death is a participation more than a transfer.

views.label: An example that moves hearts
views.case: Others claim the poem mainly shows the beauty of innocent suffering so that the beholders are changed. The confession of 53:4 to 6 certainly changes the speakers.

debates.bearing: The text asks for more than the second and third views. They are true in part, since Christ is our representative and also our example, but the vocabulary of bearing, the guilt offering and the laying of iniquity on another point beyond them to substitution. The first view includes the others rather than excluding them.

debates.question: Does the Servant 'sprinkle' or 'startle' many nations in 52:15?

views.label: He will sprinkle many nations
views.case: The verb is the one used for sprinkling blood or water in the priestly rituals, and it fits the rest of the poem, in which the Servant's work is sacrificial and purifying. The Servant is cast as a priest who cleanses the nations. Peter also speaks of believers as sprinkled with His blood, 1 Peter 1:2.

views.label: He will startle many nations
views.case: The BSB footnote notes the alternative reading 'startle'. Some scholars argue that the verb means to make leap, to startle, and that the kings shutting their mouths in the next line fits a sudden shock better than a ritual of cleansing.

debates.bearing: Both fit the context. Either the nations are cleansed by what He does, or they are stunned by it. The main point is the reversal of expectation: those who were appalled in 52:14 will see something they were not told. A reader does not need to decide to see that the Servant's exaltation reaches the Gentiles.

study.originalLanguages:
The opening description of the Servant's exaltation in 52:13 uses three verbs, translated 'raised', 'lifted up' and 'highly exalted'. The second and third are the pair Isaiah used in 6:1 for the LORD on His throne, 'high and exalted'. The verb at the start of the verse, 'will prosper', carries a second sense in the BSB footnote, 'will act wisely'. The Servant's success is the success of wise action, which is a theme that fits the rest of the poem, where His knowledge is the means of justifying many, 53:11.

The Hebrew in 53:3 and 53:4 puts two nouns together, sorrows and grief, or pains and sickness, and the verbs that follow, to carry and to bear a load, are the ones used for bearing burdens. In 53:4 He 'carried' our sorrows, and in 53:12 the same verb 'to bear', nasa, is used of the sin of many. It is the verb of Leviticus 16:22, where the goat carried the people's iniquities away. The vocabulary of the poem and of the sacrificial system overlap, so that in the first century a reader who knew Leviticus would have heard a priestly echo.

The word for 'pierced' in 53:5 comes from a root meaning to wound fatally or to pierce through, and the word for 'crushed' is a strong word for being broken. Taken together they describe violent and deadly injury. The word for 'punishment' in the same verse can mean discipline or chastisement, and the genitive 'that brought us peace' makes it the correction whose effect is our peace. The 'stripes' are wounds or bruises, in the singular, a collective sense of the whole of His suffering. This verse is quoted in 1 Peter 2:24 as 'By His stripes you are healed.'

In 53:6 the LORD 'laid upon Him' the iniquity of us all. The Hebrew verb is the hiphil of a root meaning to meet, strike or intercede, and the sense is that the LORD caused our iniquity to fall upon Him. It is the same root that appears at the end of the poem in 53:12, where the Servant 'made intercession' for the transgressors. The verb that caused sin to fall on Him and the verb that describes His pleading for sinners are one word family, so that in the Servant the burden and the prayer meet. In 53:7 the word 'afflicted' is a verb form that can describe being oppressed, and the phrase 'He did not open His mouth' is repeated, a deliberate emphasis.

The word 'guilt offering', asham, in 53:10 is a Levitical term for an offering that deals with guilt and makes restitution, as in Leviticus 5:15 and 16. Its use in the Servant Song is striking, because the sacrifice is a person. Here the one offered is the Servant's own 'soul', that is, His life. The BSB footnote to 53:10 notes that the Hebrew can also be read 'and though He makes His life a guilt offering', so the grammar leaves a small question about the subject of the verb, but the word asham is unambiguous.

The 'many' of 52:14 and 15, 53:11 and 53:12 is a repeated term in the poem. The Servant justifies 'the many', and He bears the sin of 'many', so that the many who were appalled by Him become the many who are declared righteous. The verb for 'justify' in 53:11 is a courtroom word to declare righteous, the same root as 'vindicates' in 50:8.

The Septuagint does not always follow the Hebrew closely in this chapter. The BSB footnotes record that its rendering of 53:4, 'This One bears our sins and is pained for us', is behind the citations in Matthew 8:17 and 1 Peter 2:24. And 53:8, 'In humiliation He was deprived of justice', is what the eunuch was reading in Acts 8:33. The footnotes also mark that the Dead Sea Scrolls, along with the Septuagint, add 'the light of life' to 53:11, which the traditional Hebrew text does not have.

typology.type: The guilt offering, Isaiah 53:10 and Leviticus 5:14 to 16
typology.fulfillment: A ram without blemish was brought for an offence against holy things, with restitution added, and the priest made atonement. Isaiah says that the Servant's soul is made an asham. The New Testament does not call Jesus a ram but says He offered Himself unblemished to God, Hebrews 9:14, and that by a single offering He has made perfect for all time those who are sanctified, Hebrews 10:14. The escalation is from a ram to a person and from repeated sacrifices that 'can never take away sins' to one that does, Hebrews 10:11 and 12. The type falls short in that the animal never chose, and the Servant gives His life willingly, John 10:11.

typology.type: The lamb led to the slaughter, Isaiah 53:7
typology.fulfillment: The picture of a silent lamb draws on the Passover lamb and on the daily offerings, and Jeremiah used the image of himself, Jeremiah 11:19. John the Baptist says of Jesus, 'Look, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world!', John 1:29, and Paul says that Christ our Passover lamb has been sacrificed, 1 Corinthians 5:7. In Revelation the central figure of heaven is 'a Lamb who appeared to have been slain', Revelation 5:6. Isaiah's lamb is silent before His accusers, and the Gospels record that Jesus gave no answer to the charges, as in Matthew 27:12 to 14. The type falls short because a lamb is led without understanding, whereas the Servant goes with full knowledge.

typology.type: The tender shoot and the root out of dry ground, Isaiah 53:2
typology.fulfillment: The Servant grows up unimpressively, like a sapling from parched earth. The image belongs with Isaiah 11:1 and 11:10, where a shoot springs from the stump of Jesse and a Root stands as a banner for the peoples. The New Testament calls Jesus 'the Root of David', Revelation 5:5. The correspondence is that the Davidic hope comes back not as a mighty tree but as a shoot from a stump. The escalation is that the shoot becomes a banner for the nations. It falls short only in that the shoot of Isaiah 11 is described in glory, while here the focus is on what lacked in appearance, a contrast the cross fulfils.

The Servant who sprinkles many nations is cast as the priest who cleanses. Hebrews argues that if the blood of goats and bulls sanctifies, 'how much more will the blood of Christ' purify our consciences, Hebrews 9:13 and 14. Peter speaks of believers as chosen for obedience and 'sprinkling by His blood', 1 Peter 1:2. In Christ the roles of priest and offering are united, since He sprinkles with His own blood. The type falls short because the old priests had to repeat the work and offer for themselves as well, while He needs neither.

Paul reads the one and the many together in Romans 5:19: 'through the obedience of the one man the many will be made righteous.' It is a contrast with Adam, through whose disobedience the many were made sinners. The Servant's knowledge justifies, and Paul says in Romans 4:25 that Christ was raised for our justification. The correspondence is of a single representative whose act determines the standing of many. Where Adam is a pattern of the One to come, he is also a contrast, because the grace in Christ is greater than the trespass, Romans 5:15.

study.christ:
The poem leads to Christ more directly than almost any other passage, and by several routes at once. Jesus Himself, on the night before His death, quoted its last stanza and said that this Scripture must be fulfilled in Him, 'He was numbered with the transgressors', Luke 22:37. A few hours later He was crucified between two robbers, Mark 15:27. After the resurrection He told two disciples that it was necessary for the Christ to suffer and then to enter His glory, and beginning with Moses and the Prophets He explained what was written about Himself, Luke 24:25 to 27. That pattern of suffering and then glory is exactly the pattern of Isaiah 52:13 to 53:12.

The apostles read the poem as the explanation of the cross. Peter takes the Servant's silence, sinlessness and substitution and applies them to Jesus: He committed no sin, nor was deceit found in His mouth, He did not retaliate, and He bore our sins in His body on the tree, so that by His stripes we are healed, 1 Peter 2:22 to 25. Philip, finding the eunuch reading 53:7 and 8, starts from that very passage and tells him the good news about Jesus, Acts 8:35. Matthew sees the healing ministry as the opening of the Servant's work of carrying infirmities, Matthew 8:16 and 17. Mark records that the Son of Man came to give His life 'as a ransom for many', Mark 10:45. The vocabulary of 'the many' belongs to this poem.

The Servant who is both the sacrifice and the priest is the heart of the New Testament's account of the atonement. Paul can say that 'God made Him who knew no sin to be sin on our behalf, so that in Him we might become the righteousness of God', 2 Corinthians 5:21, and that Christ was delivered over for our trespasses and raised for our justification, Romans 4:25. The one verse sums up what Isaiah said in two halves, bearing sin and justifying many. Hebrews says He 'was offered once to bear the sins of many', Hebrews 9:28.

The poem also points to Christ's exaltation. The Servant who is raised, lifted up and highly exalted at the start of the poem is the one whom Philippians says God 'exalted to the highest place' after He became obedient to death, Philippians 2:8 and 9. The verbs recall the lifted up Son of Man in John's Gospel, where 'lifted up' refers to both the cross and the glory. The crucifixion and the glory are not two separate stories in Isaiah or in John, but a single act seen from two sides.

The poem shows too that the cross was no accident. 'It was the LORD's will to crush Him', 53:10. Peter says at Pentecost that Jesus was 'delivered up by God's set plan and foreknowledge', Acts 2:23, and the early church prayed that Herod and Pilate had done what God's hand and will had decided beforehand, Acts 4:27 and 28. Paul adds that God 'did not spare His own Son but gave Him up for us all', Romans 8:32. This is not cruelty but the Father and Son acting together out of love, John 3:16, and the poem's last stanza says that the LORD takes pleasure in what prospers in the Servant's hand.

Care is needed to keep the reading honest. The poem does not name Jesus, and its first hearers could not have known the details of Calvary. What the New Testament claims is that the poem was a true prophecy of a person whose life and death filled it out, and that its wording explains what happened at the cross, which is the reason that the apostles treated the passage with such weight.
study.god:
The most striking thing the poem says about God is that He is active at the cross. The people thought the Servant was 'stricken by God', and they were right in a way they did not understand, because 'it was the LORD's will to crush Him'. The poem does not soften that. The God of this passage is no bystander who watches a righteous man suffer, nor a tyrant who needs a victim. He is the one who lays our iniquity on Him, 53:6, and who determines that the Servant's soul will be a guilt offering, 53:10. The surprising truth that the passage holds is that this is the very same God whose own Servant willingly goes to it.

God is just. The poem takes sin with full seriousness. Sin has a weight, 'iniquity', and it has to be borne. Justice is not waived, and the punishment that brings peace does not disappear. At the same time God is merciful, because the One who bears the punishment is His own. Paul sums up the same two truths in Romans 3:25 and 26: God presented Christ as the atoning sacrifice in order to show that He is righteous and that He justifies the one who has faith in Jesus. The poem is the Old Testament form of that claim.

God is also faithful to His promises. The Servant is called 'My righteous Servant', and the Servant's work 'will prosper' because the LORD vouches for it at both ends. The God of Abraham, who promised blessing to all nations, brings that promise to its goal through this Servant, whose sprinkling reaches many nations and before whom kings are silent, 52:15. The exiles who hoped for return from Babylon are given a deeper rescue than they were asking for.

God is the one who vindicates. The poem does not end at the grave. The one who was cut off from the land of the living sees His offspring and prolongs His days. 'After the anguish of His soul, He will see the light of life and be satisfied', 53:11, and the footnote notes that the 'light of life' appears in the Dead Sea Scrolls and the Septuagint. God does not leave the Servant in death. The same God who gave Him up raises Him, and the resurrection is the Father's answer to the cross.

The doctrine of God is also affected by the poem's pattern of speakers. The LORD speaks of 'My Servant' and of 'My people', and yet the arm of the LORD is revealed in the Servant. The poem leaves a tension that the New Testament resolves by saying that the Son, who is Himself God, was sent by the Father, John 1:14 and Romans 8:32. The unity of will between the Father and the Servant is the setting for the cross, and the cross is the place at which God's justice and love are shown to be one.

For worship, the poem teaches us to look at the cross with the confession of 53:4 to 6, 'we' and 'our', and 'all we like sheep'. It teaches us to be amazed that the offended party is the one who pays. It also teaches us to sing as the poem ends, with the Servant honoured: before the cross is known as a place of sorrow it is the place where the LORD's good pleasure prospers.

crossReferences.note: The prophet saw the Lord 'high and exalted'. The verbs raised, lifted up and exalted in 52:13 are the same terms, so the Servant's exaltation is described in the language used for the LORD Himself. John draws the connection in John 12:41, where he says Isaiah saw Jesus' glory.

The high priest confessed the iniquities of Israel over a live goat, and the goat carried them away. The verb to carry or bear is the same one used of the Servant in 53:4 and 53:12. The Servant is the reality to which the scapegoat pointed, bearing sin away not only symbolically but actually.

The guilt offering, a ram without blemish with restitution, is the background for the asham of 53:10. Isaiah says the Servant's soul is made such an offering. The passage shows that atonement here is not a vague idea but a defined sacrificial category in which the offence is paid for.

The Servant is 'despised and abhorred by the nation' but kings will see and rise and princes bow down. It prepares the reversal of 52:15, where kings shut their mouths. The rejection and the exaltation belong together in the Servant's story from the second Song onward.

John quotes 53:1 to explain why many did not believe Jesus despite His signs, and then says that Isaiah said these things because he saw His glory. It shows that the first Christians read the poem as a prophecy of Christ and that they linked the unbelief of Israel with the question 'Who has believed our message?'

Philip finds the eunuch reading 53:7 and 8 and, asked whether the prophet speaks of himself or someone else, begins from this passage and tells him the good news about Jesus. The earliest evangelistic use of the chapter shows how readily it was taken as a proclamation of the gospel.

Matthew applies 53:4 to Jesus' healing of the sick and the demon-possessed. 'He took on our infirmities and carried our diseases.' The Servant's bearing of sorrows begins in His ministry of healing and finds its fullest form in His death.

Peter quotes or echoes 53:9, 53:5, 53:6 and 53:12 in one paragraph. Christ did not sin, did not retaliate, bore our sins on the tree and by His stripes we are healed, and we who were like straying sheep have returned to the Shepherd. It is the most sustained apostolic reading of the poem.

Jesus says that this Scripture must be fulfilled in Him, 'And He was numbered with the transgressors', quoting 53:12 on the eve of His arrest. He claims the Servant's role and tells the disciples that what is written about Him is reaching its fulfilment.

'He was delivered over to death for our trespasses and was raised to life for our justification.' The two halves of the sentence match the two halves of the poem, in which the Servant is given over for transgressions, 53:5 and 53:12, and then justifies many, 53:11.

'God made Him who knew no sin to be sin on our behalf, so that in Him we might become the righteousness of God.' Paul states in two lines what Isaiah says in the poem: the sinless one bears what is ours, and the guilty receive what is His.

Christ 'was offered once to bear the sins of many', and will appear a second time to bring salvation. The vocabulary of bearing and of the many is taken from 53:12, and the verse also looks forward to the end of the story in the Servant's return.

study.oneStory:
Isaiah 53 is the place where the Bible's problem and the Bible's answer are set side by side most clearly. The problem begins in Genesis 3 with a man and woman who went their own way and hid from God. The poem names it again in a single sentence, 'each one has turned to his own way', and the answer, in the sentence that follows, 'the LORD has laid upon Him the iniquity of us all'. The thread that runs from the garden to the cross is that sin is real, that it has to be dealt with, and that God Himself provides the one who deals with it.

The sacrificial system of Leviticus is the next stage. The Bible spends chapters on rams, goats and bulls, and on the day each year when the high priest confessed sins over a goat. Hebrews says that these sacrifices could never take away sins, Hebrews 10:11. Isaiah 53 is where the prophets say what they were pointing to: one whose soul is a guilt offering, who does what the animals could not do. The prophets, the psalms of the righteous sufferer, and the law all find their shared goal here.

The promise to Abraham is also fulfilled. God said that all the families of the earth would be blessed through his offspring, Genesis 12:3. In 53:10 the Servant 'will see His offspring', and in 52:15 He sprinkles many nations. The blessing reaches the nations by way of a Servant who is cut off, and Paul explains how this happens in Galatians 3:13 and 14, where Christ became a curse for us so that the blessing of Abraham might come to the Gentiles.

The story also tells us about the character of God's kingdom. The kings of the earth in 52:15 shut their mouths before a man who was despised. The Servant's victory is not by force but by obedience unto death, and Jesus shows this when He rises and sends His disciples to the nations. The pattern of the first becoming last and the last first, which runs through the Gospels, is already here.

The poem looks ahead to the end of the story. The Servant divides the spoils with the strong, 53:12, and Revelation shows the slain Lamb standing at the centre of the throne and receiving worship from every nation, Revelation 5:6 to 10. Those whose iniquities He bore are the many who are declared righteous, and they share His vindication in a new creation where there is no more death or mourning or crying or pain. The story of the Bible is a story of how the God who made a good world and lost it to sin wins it back, and Isaiah 53 is the center of it, the place where the cost of that winning is told before it is paid.

sermon.title: The Sin-Bearer
sermon.why: Preached by Timothy Keller at Redeemer Presbyterian Church on February 21, 2016 directly from Isaiah 52:13-53:12, this sermon walks through the ordinariness, the violence, and the vicariousness of the Servant's suffering, showing how the passage subverts every human category of salvation and points to the substitutionary work of Christ.

quiz.q: What does it mean that the Servant's soul is made an asham, a guilt offering, in verse 10?

options.text: His death functions as the specific Levitical sacrifice for guilt requiring restitution, offered as a life rather than an animal.
options.note: Asham is the exact technical term for the guilt offering, uniquely applied here to a person.

options.text: It means His suffering was simply an unfortunate accident.
options.note: The text says it was the LORD's will, and names it with precise sacrificial vocabulary.

options.text: It refers to a burnt offering of grain, unrelated to sin.
options.note: Asham specifically denotes the guilt offering, not a grain or burnt offering.

options.text: It shows God punishing an innocent bystander at random.
options.note: It rightly senses that the Servant is innocent, but the offering language shows deliberate, purposeful substitution, not randomness.

quiz.q: How does the New Testament apply Isaiah 53 to Jesus?

options.text: Directly and repeatedly, including Philip's preaching to the Ethiopian eunuch, Peter's teaching on the cross, and Jesus' own quotation of verse 12 before His death.
options.note: Acts 8, 1 Peter 2, and Luke 22 all apply this chapter to Jesus explicitly.

options.text: It is never mentioned in the New Testament.
options.note: It is one of the most quoted Old Testament chapters in the New Testament.

options.text: Only symbolically, with no specific verses quoted.
options.note: Specific verses are quoted directly, not merely alluded to symbolically.

options.text: Only by later church tradition, never by New Testament writers themselves.
options.note: Later tradition does draw on this chapter extensively, but the New Testament writers themselves, Luke, Peter, Matthew, apply it directly and first.

quiz.q: Historically, how have Jewish interpreters read the identity of the Servant?

options.text: Variously, some reading Israel corporately, others a righteous individual or messianic figure, showing the interpretive question is real and has never been monolithic.
options.note: Honest engagement recognizes both corporate and individual Jewish readings existed.

options.text: All Jewish interpreters throughout history have read it identically as Israel and nothing else.
options.note: The corporate Israel reading is prominent and real, but this overstates uniformity; some strands, including rabbinic sources, read it messianically.

options.text: No Jewish source before Christian times ever discussed this chapter.
options.note: The chapter was read and discussed well before and alongside early Christian interpretation.

options.text: Jewish tradition unanimously identified the Servant as Jesus of Nazareth before the New Testament was written.
options.note: This is inaccurate; the messianic and Christian reading develops distinctly, especially with the New Testament writers.

quiz.q: What is the effect of the phrase 'the punishment that brought us peace was upon Him' in verse 5?

options.text: It teaches substitution: the Servant bears the punishment so that those who deserved it receive peace instead.
options.note: This is the heart of substitutionary atonement expressed in the verse.

options.text: It teaches that punishment and peace are unrelated ideas placed side by side.
options.note: The verse deliberately links the two as cause and effect.

options.text: It means the Servant made peace by avoiding all punishment.
options.note: This inverts the verse; He does not avoid punishment, He receives it fully so others gain peace.

options.text: It suggests peace comes only from human effort to be good.
options.note: The peace described flows from the Servant's suffering, not human effort.

quiz.q: What happens to the Servant after His suffering, according to verses 10-12?

options.text: He sees His offspring, prolongs His days, is satisfied, and divides the spoils with the strong, a resurrection and vindication.
options.note: These verses describe life and triumph following the Servant's death.

options.text: He simply ceases to exist with no further mention.
options.note: The text explicitly describes His continued life and exaltation afterward.

options.text: He is forgotten by those He died for.
options.note: The opposite; He justifies many and they are counted among His offspring.

options.text: He returns to obscurity with no lasting effect.
options.note: The opposite; He is allotted a portion with the great and divides the spoils, language of triumph, not obscurity.

questions: Verse 3 says we esteemed Him not, that people hid their faces from Him. Where are you tempted to be embarrassed by, or quietly hide, the suffering, crucified Christ rather than glory in Him?

Verse 6 says we all like sheep have gone astray, each one turning to his own way. What is your own way that you have followed instead of God's, and how does it feel to know your specific iniquity was laid on Him?
The Servant was silent before His accusers, verse 7, though innocent. Where is God calling you to trust Him rather than defend or vindicate yourself?
By His stripes we are healed, verse 5. What wound, physical, emotional, or spiritual, do you need to bring honestly to the healing this verse promises?
The Servant made intercession for the transgressors, verse 12, even as He was numbered among them. Who is someone difficult in your life you are being called to intercede for rather than condemn?

translationNotes.note: Guilt offering renders asham, the specific Levitical sacrifice of Leviticus 5-7; its application here to a person rather than an animal is unique in the Old Testament and central to reading this chapter as substitutionary atonement.
By His knowledge can also be read by knowledge of Him, that is, those who know Him are justified; both readings keep the emphasis on the Servant as the ground of justification.
